Part A

Four threat source categories (Table 13)

CategoryWho or whatOT example
AdversarialIntends harm: nation state, criminal group, hacktivist, insiderAll four cases in Part 2

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 15/17
Part A

Why the non adversarial sources matter

More frequent

Far more disruptions come from accidents and failures than from attacks

  • Prepare only for adversaries and you spend most of your time surprised

Shared controls

Redundancy, change control, backups, manual fallback, process monitoring

  • They work against a failed power supply and a nation state alike
  • Ukraine 2015: power came back because crews could operate breakers by hand
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 16/17
Part A

The adversaries in OT

ActorIn OT
Nation statesBehind the destructive, large scale attacks on industrial processes in the public record. Patience, custom protocol tooling, strategic goals
Criminal groupsReach OT as collateral: ransomware on IT forces a precautionary shutdown (Colonial Pipeline)
InsidersAlready have access and process knowledge. Maroochy Shire, 2000: a former contractor released sewage
HacktivistsExposed HMIs and internet reachable controllers have lowered the bar

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 18/17
Part B

Vulnerabilities and predisposing conditions

In OT the predisposing conditions do most of the work. Nobody needs a subtle flaw in a PLC that accepts any Modbus write from any address.

Vulnerability

A weakness a threat can exploit

Predisposing condition

A property that makes an incident more likely or worse, without being a defect

  • A flat network
  • A component lifetime of 10 to 15 years or more
  • A single vendor
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 19/17
Part B

Seven tables (Appendix C.2, Tables 14 to 20)

TableCategoryCovers
14Policy and procedureWhat the organization has decided and written down
15Architecture and designHow the system is laid out
16Configuration and maintenanceHow devices are set up and kept
17PhysicalWho and what can touch the equipment
18Software developmentHow device and application software was built
19Communication and network configurationHow the network is built and run
20Sensor, final element, and asset managementThe field devices, and the inventory of everything
Table 2. Table 14 is about the organization; 15 to 20 about the system. Table 20: level 0 is in scope, and not knowing what you have is a vulnerability.
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 110/17
Part B

Examples from the tables

CategoryNIST examples, condensed
Policy and procedureNo OT policy; no change management; no incident response procedures
Architecture and designNo security perimeter; control network carries non control traffic
Configuration and maintenancePatches not maintained; defaults in use; no backups; weak passwords; logs unread
PhysicalUnauthorized physical access; open USB and serial ports; no backup power
Software developmentImproper data validation; security off by default; insecure protocols
Communication and networkNo data flow controls; firewalls missing or misconfigured; plaintext; no authentication
Sensor and asset managementField devices modifiable without authentication; no asset inventory
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 111/17
Part B

Riverbend scored against the seven tables

CategoryRiverbend finding
Policy and procedureNo OT policy; vendor credentials unchanged four years; firewall logs unread; no IR procedure
Architecture and designOne subnet for everything; no DMZ; vendor access from the internet to the EWS
Configuration and maintenanceShared operator account; shared vendor credentials; no evidence of PLC backups
PhysicalSix unattended pump stations; cabinet and port security unknown
Software developmentModbus/TCP and DNP3 with no authentication
Communication and networkNo internal monitoring; cleartext; anyone can write to port 502
Sensor and asset managementNo asset inventory mentioned
Table 3. Baseline for the Week 5 risk register. Policy and configuration findings cost only attention; the rest wait for the Week 6 redesign.
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 112/17
Part B

Why OT vulnerabilities persist

  • Lifetime2008 firmware until a planned outage changes it
  • Patching windowsA fix waits for the next outage, perhaps annual
  • Vendor controlContracts forbid changes; vendor remote access is itself a condition
  • Insecure by designNo patch adds authentication to Modbus; the remedy is architectural
  • VisibilityNo inventory, no monitoring, no idea which weaknesses apply (Table 20)
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 113/17
Part B

How OT vulnerabilities are disclosed

CISA ICS advisories, for example ICSA-24-123-01. Vendors publish a matching notice. Reading advisories is routine in any OT security role: learn the anatomy once.

Anatomy of a CISA ICS advisory

SectionTells youYou do
Executive summaryCVSS, remotely exploitable?, vendor, product, CWEIs it in my inventory, how bad?

MitigationsVendor's fixed version; CISA standing recommendationsCan I patch? If not, which recommendations do I have?

The CVSS score is an IT score

Table 16 says why

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 116/17

Summary

  • Four threat sources. The non adversarial ones are more frequent and share controls with attack defense
  • Seven vulnerability tables. In OT the predisposing conditions do most of the damage. Riverbend has findings in every one
  • Vulnerabilities persist: lifetime, patching windows, vendor control, insecure design, poor visibility
  • Advisories: an IT score, a patch you may not be able to apply, and standing recommendations that are this course
  • Next: Part 2, four incidents and the anatomy of an OT attack
